This is so vague that I should be posting it in /v/halfbaked, but here goes anyway...

From a UX perspective, Reddit's "up" and "down" arrows are a poor decision unless they are intended to represent "I agree" and "I disagree." I've heard a lot of discussion here about trying to change voting behavior to be more along the lines of "this is interesting" vs "this is off topic or is otherwise not a meaningful contribution," but I still see a lot of downvotes based on opinion. I think people are naturally drawn towards downvoting content they don't like, as most of us feel a visceral reaction when we see content that makes us angry or uncomfortable. If there is a quick and easy way to express disagreement, we'll take it.

The effect of this is that downvotes on Reddit -- and increasingly on Voat -- have become like shaking your head in disapproval. Unfortunately, both of those behaviors tend to foster animosity and shut down real discussion. I think we can do better.

Facebook has a similar problem. A while ago, there was a failed campaign on Facebook to get a "dislike" button implemented. One reason for this is that users don't feel that "like" is appropriate when (for instance) someone's dog dies, but they feel a sense of cognitive dissonance -- they always "like" their friend's posts, but now they have nothing to click! This is fundamentally misunderstanding the purpose of the like button, which is intended to express that you "like" the post itself and want to encourage more of the same. Facebook can't seem to fix this misunderstanding, no matter how many times they try to tell users what it means to "like" something. In contrast, as much hate as Google gets for G+, they did it right with the "+1" button -- everyone there seems willing to +1 interesting content, even if they don't agree with it or see it as a positive thing.

What I'd like to suggest is that we change the up/down arrows into something that better reflects their intended usage. This is a real UX challenge, and I don't know the best way to go about it. What I do know is that we ought to reconsider everything about Reddit's up/down arrows: the placement (both the placement relative to the link and the placement relative to each other), the icon (should we have a different icon? Should we use text?), the size, the color, and the function (should "downvotes" require extra effort?).

Any thoughts on this? I feel that we have to either try to make some changes or stop complaining about "misuse" of downvotes. When a feature is designed to encourage a certain form of usage, you can't really complain when people use it as it was designed!

I loved reading RPG rulebooks, many of which I'd never actually play. I used to tell people this but they scoffed. They scoffed at me, voaters. Maybe because of the way I would claim in my pretentious early teenage way, "a novel might tell a story, but an RPG builds an entire world."

I remember Demon: The Fallen had a particularly compelling setting. A bum-lousy system, but a great back story with something like a hundred pages of fiction from various perspectives included in the rulebook. The Van Richten's Guides for Ravenloft were amazing and I treasure my copies to this day. Teenagers from Outer Space, Mutant Chronicles, Paranoia; all much-read and little-played.

I have a similar relationship with Eclipse Phase. I own all the books in hardcopy and I love the setting but I've only ever run a single one shot for it. Doesn't mean I don't love it, but I would need a different group dynamic to want to actually run it continuously.

I like reading rulebooks for the rules personally :) I have in my youth tried to create a few different systems and I'm very interested to see how different people solve different problems. It's always interesting to see how different people and companies tackle character creation, progress, combat, etc.
